title: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges
transcript: A digit has a value and a position. The digit sum forgets the positions, but a count of written digits must consider every position. Break a range count into the ones, tens and hundreds places, then add those separate counts.

The AMC can ask how often a digit is written. Work in complete blocks, then inspect the last incomplete block. In Mawa primary application practice, digit sum restrictions can be combined with range restrictions. Use place value to prove which cases count.
What remainder does four hundred and eight leave after division by nine? Use its digits to find the remainder without long division. Ten and one hundred both leave remainder one when divided by nine.

One hundred, ten and one each contribute the same remainder as one. The digit sum is four plus zero plus eight, which is twelve. The remainder of that sum is three, which is also the remainder of four hundred and eight.
Write every whole number from one through two hundred and eighty-nine. How many times do you write the digit five? Each occurrence counts separately. Track the ones, tens and hundreds separately.

In the ones place every complete block of ten contributes one occurrence, with a possible extra at the end. The ones total is twenty-nine. In the tens place, each complete hundred contains one run of ten occurrences. Include any matching part of the last hundred. That gives thirty. In the hundreds place, only the block starting at five hundred could match. It contributes zero. Adding the three totals gives fifty-nine written occurrences.

Write the multiples of nine from one hundred through seven hundred and ninety-nine, including any endpoint that is a multiple. Count every written five. Split the appearances among the three places. A number can contribute in more than one place.

Fix the ones digit at five. For each hundreds digit, choose a tens digit so the three digits add to a multiple of nine. Each required remainder for the tens digit gives one choice, except remainder zero gives zero and nine. Here the hundreds digit four gives that double choice. The tens count is the same, since swapping the two end digits preserves the digit sum and the hundreds range. Each of these places contributes eight.

For the hundreds place, fix the hundreds digit instead. The hundred block starting at five hundred contributes eleven occurrences, one for every multiple of nine in that block. Add the three position counts. An occurrence in one position is different from an occurrence in another, even in the same number. The total is twenty-seven.

If a number contains the requested digit twice, it contributes two occurrences. Compare counting numbers with counting written digits. Digits zero and nine both have remainder zero on division by nine. Include both when zero is permitted in the position.

Write whether you need a sum, a number of valid integers or a count of written occurrences. Record the exact range. Use place-value blocks or digit-sum restrictions to organise the work. Check an endpoint and a number with a repeated digit before totalling.
